abstracts.doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11296547/v1: Abstract Objective: Standard guidelines for neurodegenerative diseases rely on cohort-level criteria, frequently misclassifying isolated atypical phenotypes. This study tests whether atypical variants mirror topographically determined systemic central nervous system (CNS) conditions rooted in pre-existing vulnerability. Methods: Using "reverse-matching", phenotypes from six atypical cases—representing motor neuron disease/frontotemporal dementia ( N = 3) and multiple system atrophy, parkinsonian type ( N = 3)—were mapped onto a protein-agnostic network matrix (onto-phylogenetic coordinate system, OPC; Geser 2026). Spatial network recruitment was quantified using Jaccard coefficients ( J ). Spearman rank correlations ( ρ ) evaluated systemic hierarchies against conventional reference matrices (Geser 2008 cohort, TDP-43, N = 31; Jellinger 2005 cohort, α-synuclein, N = 42). Model comparison was performed using Steiger’s Z -test. Results: Conventional, cohort-based staging exhibited profound topographical inversion, yielding negative correlations for TDP-43 ( ρ = -0.9113, p ρ = -0.8660, p = 0.003) sub-cohorts. Conversely, the novel OPC system resolved this mismatch, reversing the correlation into a highly precise positive range (TDP-43: ρ = 0.9113, p R 2 = 0.83; α-synuclein: ρ = 0.8660, p = 0.003, R 2 = 0.75). In the combined pool ( N = 18 data pairs), the OPC model achieved strong global validation ( ρ = 0.8825, p R 2 = 0.78; Steiger Z = -6.497, p J = 1.00). Interpretation: Atypical variants are not statistical outliers but topographically determined systemic states reflecting inherent CNS vulnerability. Clinical anomalies serve as highly sensitive, topographically anchored early indicators ("red flags") of underlying proteinopathies.
